items.title: booking-agent
items.tagline: Appointments booked by chatting: the assistant finds and holds the time, the customer confirms it with a button, and PostgreSQL makes double booking impossible.
items.description: Conversational booking in .NET 10 with Claude Haiku 5.5: narrow tools the assistant cannot use to confirm, holds that run out, reminders through an outbox, sign-in with an emailed code, and a live panel showing why each booking was made.

metrics.label: eval conversations ending as expected
bookings confirmed or cancelled by the assistant
simultaneous requests for one slot: only one gets it
model cost per conversation

video.caption: 75 seconds with Claude Haiku 5.5 (Spanish captions): the customer books in the chat on the left, and the booking appears at once in the clinic's panel on the right.

gallery.alt: The chat: the customer asks for a cleaning on Monday morning, the assistant offers 8:00, 9:00 and 10:00 and holds 10:00 as a card with a countdown and the Confirmar button
gallery.caption: The assistant holds the time; only the customer confirms it, with the card's button.

gallery.alt: The clinic's panel with Dra. Ana López's week and the 10:00 booking held, in amber and marked IA
gallery.caption: It appears at once in the clinic's panel, not yet confirmed.

gallery.alt: The booking's details in the panel: the whole conversation and every model and tool call, with tokens, latency and a total cost of USD 0.0024
gallery.caption: The why of each booking: the conversation and every step of the assistant, with its cost.

caseStudy.context: Clinics and salons lose hours on the phone booking appointments. A chatbot that books by itself trades that problem for others: double bookings, appointments nobody asked for, and made-up answers. The goal was a useful assistant that cannot do harm: one that understands "el lunes en la mañana", searches the real calendar, and leaves the final decision to the customer.
constraints: The assistant never confirms or cancels: it proposes, and the person acts with a button
No double booking, even when fifty people ask for the same slot at once
Spanish relative dates resolved on the server, on the business's time zone
Notices and reminders that are never lost, and never announce what was not saved
A visible cost per conversation, capped per conversation and per day
architecture: Eight tools, each a thin adapter over a use case the booking form also uses: the assistant can do nothing the form cannot, and an architecture test enforces it.
Holding a slot takes it for five minutes in PostgreSQL, under an exclusion constraint on time ranges. The confirmation token goes to the chat's card, never to the model.
Notices are written to an outbox in the same transaction as the booking, and a dispatcher sends them by email and to an in-app inbox, with retries.
Customers sign in with a six-digit code sent by email to see, move or cancel their appointments; the session lives in an HttpOnly cookie.
Every booking change is announced over SignalR, and the clinic's panel reloads the week at once. Each booking the assistant made shows its conversation and steps, with tokens and cost.

decisions.title: The person confirms, not the assistant
decisions.rationale: Having a model decide whether "sí, pero…" means yes is a risk and a cost. A button with a one-time token is deterministic.
decisions.tradeoff: Someone who types "sí" still has to press the button; the assistant reminds them.

decisions.title: Double booking is prevented by PostgreSQL
decisions.rationale: Check-then-insert loses the race; an exclusion constraint does not, whether the booking comes from the chat, the form or a bug.
decisions.tradeoff: Saves for the same professional are queued, under a transaction lock.

decisions.title: Evaluated like software, on the database
decisions.rationale: 28 scripted conversations are scored on what ends up stored, not on what the assistant says: whether it held the right time, and whether it changed anything it should not.
decisions.tradeoff: A run against the real model costs about USD 0.07, so it is started by hand; CI runs a free oracle.

results: With Claude Haiku 5.5, all 28 eval conversations end as expected: bookings, conflicts, moves, cancellations and manipulation attempts.
No booking confirmed or cancelled by the assistant, and no slot held that the calendar had not offered first.
Fifty simultaneous requests for one slot: one gets it and the other 49 receive the nearest free times, in about a second.
The first run scored 0.76: the transcripts showed "mañana" was not resolved in a container without culture data. It was fixed and is now covered by the tests.
An end-to-end Playwright test walks the chat, the live panel, the emailed code and a cancellation on every push, with no API key and no cost.

items.title: docs-assistant
items.tagline: An AI support assistant that answers from your documents, cites every answer, and hands the conversation to a person when it doesn't know.
items.description: An embeddable RAG chatbot in .NET 10: hybrid search in PostgreSQL with pgvector, Claude Haiku behind a swappable port, and a 9 KB widget that installs with one line.

metrics.label: retrieval hit@5 on a 54-question bilingual eval
prompt-injection attacks resisted
model cost per 1,000 questions
embeddable widget

video.caption: 75 seconds on a demo store. On-screen text in Spanish, answers by Claude Haiku 5.5.

caseStudy.context: Small businesses answer the same questions all day, and generic chatbots make up answers that the business then has to correct. The goal was an assistant a customer can trust: it answers only from the business’s own documents, shows where each answer came from, and when it cannot answer, it says so and passes the conversation to a person.
constraints: No invented answers: abstaining beats guessing
Questions and documents in different languages, Spanish and English
A small, visible cost per answer, with hard spending caps
It has to embed in any website without breaking its styles
Several businesses on one deployment, each seeing only its own data
architecture: Documents (PDF, DOCX, Markdown and web pages) are split along their structure and indexed twice in PostgreSQL: as vectors, for meaning across languages, and as full text, for exact words, numbers and names.
A question searches both indexes and the two rankings are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Passages shaped like injected instructions are quarantined before they reach the model.

Below a measured similarity floor the assistant abstains without calling the model. Otherwise Claude answers from those passages only and cites them as [1], [2]; the citations are validated before the answer streams to the widget over SSE.
The widget is framework-free TypeScript inside a Shadow DOM: 9 KB, one script tag, and styles that never leak into the host page.

decisions.title: Abstain before calling the model
decisions.rationale: When retrieval finds nothing similar enough, the answer is “I can’t find that” plus a person, decided in code at zero cost.
decisions.tradeoff: A few answerable questions are refused when retrieval misses. The eval tracks that rate, so the floor is tuned on data rather than taste.

decisions.title: Hybrid search, not vectors alone
decisions.rationale: Vectors handle meaning and cross-language questions; full text catches the prices, codes and names that embeddings blur. Guaranteeing one vector hit in the fused list raised cross-lingual hit@5 from 86% to 95%.
decisions.tradeoff: Two indexes to maintain and a fusion step to tune, though both live in the PostgreSQL the app already needs.

decisions.title: The model behind a port, with spending guards
decisions.rationale: Claude sits behind Microsoft.Extensions.AI, so the model is a configuration choice, and an extractive mode works with no model at all. The evals refuse to spend without an explicit flag, a call cap and a cost cap.
decisions.tradeoff: A thin abstraction layer to keep current, in exchange for never being locked to one provider or surprised by a bill.

results: Retrieval finds the right passage for 98% of the 54 eval questions, and for 95% when the question and the document are in different languages.
With Claude Haiku 5.5: 0 invalid citations, abstention on 100% of the unanswerable questions, and USD 0.33 per 1,000 questions.
12 of 12 prompt-injection attacks resisted (8 direct, 4 hidden inside documents), while 0 of the 54 real questions were wrongly refused.
Every number comes from an eval in the repository that anyone can rerun, and CI fails if retrieval drops below its thresholds.

items.title: invoice-extractor
items.tagline: Turns photos and PDFs of invoices into rows ready for the books: Claude reads them, accounting rules check every number, and what does not add up goes to a person.
items.description: Invoice and receipt reading in .NET 10 with Claude Haiku 5.5: deterministic validation after the model, a queue in PostgreSQL, human review beside the original, and export to Excel and CSV.

metrics.label: false auto-approvals in the evals
planted errors sent to review, none approved
accuracy on total, date, tax id and number, with the retry
model cost per document

video.caption: 75 seconds with Claude Haiku 5.5: three of the built-in examples, two approved by the rules, one corrected by a person. On-screen text in Spanish.

gallery.alt: The review screen: a photographed receipt on the left and, on the right, the fields read, with the total flagged in red because subtotal plus tax does not give it
gallery.caption: What does not add up goes to review: the original alongside, the failing field flagged.

gallery.alt: A batch of three documents: a PDF and a scan approved automatically, and a photo that needs review
gallery.caption: A batch of three: two pass every rule and are approved on their own.

gallery.alt: Dashboard with 3 documents, 67% approved automatically, the total model cost and the average cost per document
gallery.caption: The dashboard: how many are approved on their own, and what reading each one costs.

caseStudy.context: Many small businesses still type their invoices into the books by hand. A language model can read them, but it is sometimes confidently wrong, and a misread invoice in the books is worse than one left out. The goal was a reader you can trust: one that approves only what it can check, and sends the rest to a person with what they need to decide quickly.
constraints: Nothing is approved on the model's word alone: every reading is checked by rules
Tilted photos, poor scans, thermal receipts and PDFs, in Spanish and English
Tax rules per country: Nicaragua's RUC and VAT, Mexico's RFC and VAT, and a generic profile
Exact amounts end to end: decimals, never floating point
A visible cost per document and a daily spending cap
architecture: Each file is checked on its own (real format, size, pages) and recognised by its hash: uploading the same one twice does not cost twice.
A PostgreSQL queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and a lease hands documents to the workers: each one is read exactly once, even if a worker crashes.
Claude Haiku 5.5 reads a digital PDF's text or the image of a scan or photo, with structured output against a JSON Schema. Amounts travel as text and become decimals without ever being a double.

Deterministic rules decide: the lines add up to the subtotal, subtotal plus tax gives the total, the rate exists in that country and the tax id has its format. A failing reading is read once more with the errors as a hint; if it still fails, it goes to human review.
A Next.js web app, in Spanish and English, shows each document's status live, the review beside the original and a cost dashboard, and exports to Excel and CSV.

decisions.title: The model proposes, the rules decide
decisions.rationale: Arithmetic and formats can be checked without AI. A reading that does not add up is never approved on its own, however confident it looks, and the model can also say it is unsure of a field.
decisions.tradeoff: Rules catch inconsistencies, not every error: a misread value that still adds up would pass. The evals count those cases, and so far there are none.

decisions.title: One retry, with the errors as a hint
decisions.rationale: Most misreadings are a digit or a letter. Told which rule failed, the model fixes it: on the hard set, tax-id accuracy goes from 91.7% to 100%.
decisions.tradeoff: About 50% more cost on hard documents, and the ones that are really wrong are paid for twice before they reach a person.

decisions.title: A queue in PostgreSQL, not a broker
decisions.rationale: SKIP LOCKED and a lease give exactly-once processing with the database the app already has. A test with four workers and a hundred documents proves it.
decisions.tradeoff: It polls the database every few seconds and has a throughput ceiling, far above what an accounting office uploads.

results: On 42 synthetic eval documents, with Claude Haiku 5.5 and the retry: 100% accuracy on total, date, tax id and number, and no false auto-approval.
The 7 documents with deliberately planted errors end in human review in every run.
Without the retry, the hard set misses the tax-id pass mark (91.7% against 95%). That failure is published alongside the successes.
USD 0.00065 per document on the standard set and USD 0.00097 on the hard one, retries included.
A Playwright end-to-end test drives the real app (upload, review, approval and Excel) on every push, with recorded model answers: no API key and no cost.

items.title: talent-mcp
items.tagline: An MCP server in C# that gives AI agents typed, secured tools for recruiting, built on the session-less 2026-07-28 protocol revision.
items.description: Six typed tools for job search, candidate-fit scoring and skill extraction, over stateless Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1 + PKCE, and the same six over stdio as a dotnet tool. Published on NuGet.

metrics.label: typed tools, each behind its own OAuth scope
LLM calls: deterministic, zero-cost scoring
cold start of the dotnet tool, measured in CI
test levels that gate every merge

gallery.alt: MCP Inspector showing the server’s confirmation request before rejecting a candidate, with the reason on record
gallery.caption: Before an action that cannot be undone, the server asks for confirmation, with the reason on record.

gallery.alt: MCP Inspector showing a candidate-fit score of 85 with the skill, seniority and location components
gallery.caption: An explainable score: 85 out of 100, with the reason behind each component.

gallery.alt: MCP Inspector listing the server’s tools and the result of a job search
gallery.caption: The system as tools an agent can call, each with its permission and its rules.

caseStudy.context: AI agents are only as useful as the tools they can call safely. The 2026-07-28 revision of the Model Context Protocol removed sessions and server-initiated requests, which breaks the usual ways of paging results and of asking the user for confirmation. talent-mcp is a reference server for that revision, in a domain where mistakes are costly: recruiting.
constraints: No server sessions: any replica must be able to serve any request
Destructive actions need explicit confirmation, without server-initiated requests
Authorization per tool: read, write and destructive scopes are not interchangeable
Reproducible results, so the scoring can serve as a test oracle
architecture: Clean Architecture with the dependency rule enforced by architecture tests in CI. Domain references nothing; Application holds the use cases and ports; Infrastructure holds the EF Core, Keycloak and OpenTelemetry adapters.
The six tools live in one project that two hosts share verbatim: an ASP.NET Core Streamable HTTP server shipped as a container image, and a stdio host shipped as a dotnet tool.

State between calls travels as a signed, time-limited handle passed back as an ordinary tool argument. The client’s trace context arrives in _meta, so one trace follows the agent’s call through the tool down to every PostgreSQL command, with per-tool latency and error metrics alongside.

decisions.title: No LLM inside the server
decisions.rationale: Scoring and skill normalization are pure functions, so the server needs no API keys, costs nothing to run and returns the same answer every time.
decisions.tradeoff: Less flexible than asking a model; the agent on the other side brings the language understanding.

decisions.title: Signed handles instead of sessions
decisions.rationale: Pagination state is encoded, signed and time-limited inside the handle itself, so the HTTP host scales horizontally with no sticky sessions and no shared cache.
decisions.tradeoff: Handles are opaque and they expire; a client that holds one too long has to search again.

decisions.title: Tools registered explicitly, not by assembly scan
decisions.rationale: A trimmed build that silently drops its tools answers -32601 with no crash and no error log. Explicit registration, plus a conformance test that asserts all six tools by name, makes that failure loud.
decisions.tradeoff: Adding a tool means touching the registration as well as writing the tool.

results: Published on NuGet as a reusable toolkit library and as the talent-mcp dotnet tool, with a container image on GHCR.
Five test levels gate every merge, from architecture rules to end-to-end runs through OAuth and PostgreSQL.
The Tasks store is verified to survive a database restart, recovering its connections in about a second.
Cold start of the installed dotnet tool measured in CI at 323 ms.

items.title: claude-pr-review-bot
items.tagline: A pull request reviewer for GitHub Actions that asks Claude for one document of findings, and can only ever comment.
items.description: C# on .NET 10. Structured output against a JSON Schema, a single read_file tool, findings filtered against the lines GitHub accepts, and one review per run. It never approves, requests changes or blocks a merge.

metrics.label: bugs flagged in a real demo pull request
measured cost of that review on Claude Haiku 5.5
permissions to approve, block or merge
tool: read_file, fetched by SHA from the API

gallery.alt: The bot’s inline comment on a pull request: a Dictionary cache in a singleton service is not thread-safe
gallery.caption: On the exact line: a cache shared by concurrent requests, and the stale orders it would serve.

gallery.alt: The bot’s comment on a catch-all that turns every payment error into a declined charge
gallery.caption: It applies the project’s own rule: a timeout from the processor is not a decline.

gallery.alt: The bot’s comment on a line that writes the payments API key to the console
gallery.caption: A secret written to stdout, caught before it reaches a log in production.

gallery.alt: The pull request conversation with the bot’s review summary: three blockers, comments only
gallery.caption: One review per run, with a summary that says it only comments.

caseStudy.context: The obvious AI reviewer gives the model a post-comment tool and executes each call as it arrives. That costs a round trip per finding, can leave half a review behind when a call times out, and never gives the code a moment to see the whole set and decide it is noise. An early version left 47 comments on one pull request, most of them on generated files.
constraints: It must review pull requests from forks, which needs secrets under pull_request_target
Contributor code must never run next to the API key
A prompt injection inside a diff must not be able to approve or block anything
A predictable, visible cost per pull request
architecture: The bot fetches the changed files and their patches from the GitHub API and parses the hunks into the set of lines GitHub will accept a comment on.

Claude receives the diff as untrusted content and returns its findings as one document that conforms to a JSON Schema. When a hunk is a keyhole, it can call read_file, which fetches the file at the head SHA through a path check.
A filter drops findings outside the diff, keeps the most severe one per line and caps the total. Then a single COMMENT review is posted, and every dropped finding is logged.

decisions.title: Findings as data, not actions
decisions.rationale: Structured output returns the whole set at once, so the code can filter, deduplicate and cap it before anything reaches GitHub, and a failure posts nothing instead of half a review.
decisions.tradeoff: The review appears all at once at the end of the run instead of comment by comment.

decisions.title: Comment-only by construction
decisions.rationale: The GitHub client has five methods, and none of them can approve, request changes or merge. The worst a prompt injection can do is make the bot go quiet.
decisions.tradeoff: It cannot enforce anything; a team that wants a blocking gate keeps it in its own CI.

decisions.title: Built from source on every run
decisions.rationale: The composite action compiles the bot at the pinned ref, so the code reviewing your pull request is exactly the code in the repository.
decisions.tradeoff: About a minute per run; a Docker action would be faster but less transparent.

results: On a real demo pull request, Claude Haiku 5.5 flagged all three bugs it introduced (a non-thread-safe cache, a catch-all that turns timeouts into declines, an API key written to stdout) in one call, for USD 0.0009.
About USD 0.12 per 400-line pull request on Claude Opus 5 and about USD 0.05 on Sonnet 5, with input, output and cache-read tokens logged per turn.
A cached system prompt, plus a built-in ignore list for lockfiles and generated code that more than halved the average diff sent to the model.
A dry-run mode with fixture findings exercises the whole pipeline in CI on every push, with no API key.
The design is explained in a DEV.to article, in English and in Spanish.

about.title: About Me
about.subtitle: Get to know me better
about.bio: Senior Software Engineer with 15+ years building and modernizing .NET systems for multinational companies and the public sector. Today I pair that foundation with applied AI: RAG assistants that cite their sources, MCP servers for agents and Claude-powered code review, each measured with quality and cost evals. I work end to end, from architecture and backend to frontend, CI/CD and the cloud, and I lead teams with agile practices.

expertise.ai: RAG assistants on PostgreSQL and pgvector, MCP servers and agents with Claude behind Microsoft.Extensions.AI. Evals in CI, spending guards and prompt-injection defenses.
expertise.frontend: Modern web applications with React, Next.js, TypeScript, and Angular. Expertise in building responsive, accessible, and performant user interfaces.
expertise.backend: Scalable server-side solutions with .NET, Node.js, and SQL databases. Experience with RESTful APIs, microservices, and data processing.
expertise.cloud: Cloud infrastructure on AWS and Azure. Proficient in Docker, CI/CD pipelines, and DevOps practices for high-availability systems.
